passage: In the small-town school's exam hall the fan turned slowly, and half the class was quietly copying. Himani counted six slips passing along the back row, and Afreen, beside her, tilted her paper without a word. Himani stared at her own blank answer to question four. If half the class does it, she thought, then it's basically normal. Nobody is getting caught, so what's the harm? She glanced at Afreen's paper, then at the invigilator reading a newspaper, and copied the whole answer. The thought of the few who had studied for weeks and would now score the same or less drifted in and drifted out. She would think about that later. By the bell her sheet was full, and she felt only relief, not the pride a full sheet used to bring.

qa.q: How many slips did Himani count in the back row?
qa.a: Himani counted six slips passing along the back row.

qa.q: What was Himani telling herself, and what did she feel at the end?
qa.a: She told herself it was basically normal because half the class does it, and at the end she felt only relief, not pride.

qa.q: What could Himani have done differently?
qa.a: She could have written what she knew and asked the teacher for help later, since a crowd doing something does not make it fair to those who studied.

qa.q: How might a classmate who studied for weeks see the copying?
qa.a: A classmate who studied may feel frustrated and unfairly treated, since copying blurs the value of honest effort.

grounding: A student notes that half the class copies and decides it does not matter, using the crowd as an excuse instead of weighing fairness.

In the corridor of her school in Istanbul, Zeynep watched half her class pass round photos of the homework answers on their phones before the history quiz. Camila, her closest friend, was among them, and Zeynep had started copying some too.
It had bothered her the first time. Now she barely noticed. When her mother asked why her quiz marks were suddenly so high, Zeynep shrugged. “Everyone does it. If I don't, I'm the only one losing marks.”
She didn't think about the three students who never looked at the photos, or about the quizzes being meant to show the teacher what they had actually learned. It was easier to let the standard slide with the crowd.
Then the end-of-term exam came, in the exam hall, with no phones allowed. Zeynep stared at a question on the Ottoman trade routes she had “answered” four times that term. She couldn't remember any of it. Beside her, one of the three who had never copied was writing steadily.

qa.q: How were the homework answers shared?
qa.a: As photos on their phones, passed round before the history quiz.

qa.q: How did Zeynep feel about the copying by now, compared with the first time?
qa.a: It had bothered her at first, but now she felt indifferent, calm about it because everyone did it.

qa.q: What could Zeynep have thought about instead of "everyone does it"?
qa.a: Whether it was fair to the three who didn't copy, and whether she was actually learning, before following the crowd.

qa.q: How was the exam for the student who never copied?
qa.a: That student could write steadily, having actually learned the material, while the copiers struggled.

grounding: Shows a student using the fact that half the class copies as an excuse, letting the standard slide without weighing fairness, and paying for it in the exam.

At the coaching institute, the Saturday weekly test had one tired assistant for sixty students. Gurpreet showed Shankar how most of the back rows kept the answer key on their phones under the desk.
Shankar hesitated the first week. By the third week he had stopped hesitating. “Half the room does it,” he told himself. “The rank list is fake anyway. If I don't, I'm just the fool at the bottom.”
He didn't think about what the tests were for, telling each student where they stood before the real entrance exam, or about the boy in the front row who scored low every week because he actually did the paper alone.
In December the institute ran a full mock in a hall with phones collected at the door. Shankar, ranked eighth for weeks, came fifty-first. The boy from the front row came ninth.
Gurpreet came forty-seventh. Neither of them said much on the bus home.

qa.q: Where did Shankar rank in the December mock?
What was Shankar telling himself by the third week, and how did it make him feel?
qa.a: That half the room does it and the rank list is fake, which let him feel comfortable instead of guilty.

qa.q: What else could Shankar have done in the first week?
qa.a: Do the test alone and treat a low score as honest feedback, perhaps asking a teacher what to work on.

qa.q: How might the boy from the front row see the December results?
qa.a: He would likely feel vindicated and proud, his honest weekly work finally showing as real progress.

grounding: Shows a student using the crowd as an excuse to copy in weekly tests, letting the standard slide until an honest mock reveals the cost.
